definition: The perceived benefits a customer is willing to pay for, not simply the cost of producing the product or service.
The residual left when the cost of creating value is subtracted from the value created: Value Created minus Cost of Creating Value equals Margin.

The full range of internal activities a company undertakes to bring a product or service from initial conception to end use and beyond, an inward-looking umbrella concept in contrast to the outward-looking supply chain.
A framework mapping a firm's internal activities — five ordered primary activities and four unordered support activities — into a single arrow that ends in margin.
The five value-chain activities that directly develop inputs into outputs, happen in a fixed order, and are the source of cost advantage.
The four value-chain activities that make the primary activities more efficient, have no fixed order, and are the source of differentiation advantage.
The primary activity of receiving, storing and distributing the inputs a business uses, such as receiving a raw-material delivery.
The primary activity of transforming inputs into finished products or services, such as cooking meals or manufacturing phones.
The primary activity of delivering the finished product or service to customers, such as running a delivery service or shipping to retailers.
The primary activity of creating awareness of a product and persuading customers to buy it, such as through advertising or in-store promotions.
The primary activity of supporting the customer after the sale, such as through warranty, tech support or loyalty programs.
The support activity covering company structure, finance, legal and strategy, such as the accounting system.
The support activity of hiring, training and retaining people, such as employee onboarding.
The support activity of innovation, R&D and building the tools that improve a process, such as a POS system, as distinct from Operations, which runs the transformation itself.

The support activity of deciding and acquiring resources such as raw materials or tools — negotiating and choosing suppliers — as distinct from Inbound Logistics, which is the physical handling once the input is already owned.
Designing, running, measuring and improving the processes that transform inputs into outputs.
A sequence of activities that transforms inputs into outputs, one level more detailed than a value-chain activity.
A framework — Supplier, Input, Process, Output, Customer — used to define what is inside and outside a process boundary before mapping it.
A process step that changes the product or service in a way the customer values, such as brewing the coffee.
A process step that consumes resources without creating value and could be deleted with nothing lost but cost and delay, such as waiting for an unavailable cup.
The maximum output a process or resource can produce in a given period, always expressed as a quantity per unit of time, such as 25 drinks per hour.
The step in a serial process with the lowest capacity, which constrains the throughput of the whole process.
Demand divided by capacity, expressed as a percentage, showing how much of a process's available capacity is being used.
The number of units a process completes per unit of time.
The number of units currently in a process at a given moment.
In a stable process, Work-in-process equals Throughput Rate multiplied by Flow Time (WIP = Throughput x Flow Time).
A performance signal derived from a business objective through a process driver to a measurable target, used to understand, decide and improve, not just a raw number.
A process type producing unique, one-time work in low volume with high variety, such as constructing a building.
A process type producing custom, small-batch work, such as a tailor shop.
A process type producing medium-volume, repeated batches of output, such as a bakery.
A process type producing high-volume, standardized output, such as an assembly line.
A process type running 24/7 at high volume with no variety, such as an oil refinery.
Business Process Model and Notation, a flowchart-based OMG standard since 2005 (now BPMN 2.0) used for both conceptual and executable process models.
An atomic, indivisible unit of work in BPMN, drawn as a plain rounded rectangle.
A compound BPMN activity, drawn as a rounded rectangle with a + marker, that expands into its own process with its own start and end events.
Something that happens during a BPMN process — a trigger or a result that starts, interrupts or ends the flow — named in "something done" (past-participle) form.
A BPMN element that controls how sequence flows converge and diverge, needed only when the flow actually requires control.
An exclusive BPMN gateway whose split takes exactly one outgoing branch and whose join proceeds once that one branch has completed.
A parallel BPMN gateway whose split takes every outgoing branch at once and whose join waits until all incoming branches have completed.
An inclusive BPMN gateway whose split can take one or several outgoing branches depending on conditions, and whose join waits only for the branches actually taken.
A solid line with a filled arrowhead showing the order of activities within the same BPMN process or pool.
A dashed line with an open circle and open arrowhead showing the exchange of messages between different BPMN pools.
A flow of materials, information and money across suppliers, manufacturers and customers, coordinated across multiple organisations rather than managed within one firm.
Managing the flow of materials, information and money across a supply chain efficiently and strategically.
A supply-chain strategy that prioritises cost and high utilisation for stable, predictable demand, such as Walmart or Big C.
A supply-chain strategy that prioritises speed and availability for uncertain, short-life-cycle demand, such as Zara.
A supply-chain strategy that prioritises flexibility and adaptability for highly uncertain, varied demand, using small batches, flexible suppliers and postponement, such as Louis Vuitton or Dell.
A supply-chain strategy that pushes to forecast upstream and pulls to real demand downstream, placing a push-pull boundary and segmenting customers and products to balance cost and responsiveness.
The cross-functional process of estimating future customer demand — by volume, timing, location and segment — to support inventory, production, sourcing and transport decisions.
The shortfall that results when actual demand exceeds the forecast, causing lost sales, expedited shipments and dissatisfied customers.
An approach triggered by forecast in which inventory is produced and shipped in advance of demand, best when demand is predictable and lead times are long.
An approach triggered by actual customer demand or order in which inventory is built only after demand is known, best when demand is uncertain and customisation matters.
The point in a supply chain where the process switches from forecast-driven push to demand-driven pull, typically where postponement and final customisation happen.
A bullwhip cause in which large, infrequent orders rather than small, frequent ones create artificial demand spikes upstream.
The phenomenon in which small changes in customer demand create progressively larger order fluctuations further upstream in the supply chain.
A supply-chain simulation with four roles (Retailer, Wholesaler, Distributor, Manufacturer) across 20 weekly rounds that demonstrates how withholding demand information amplifies the bullwhip effect.
A model showing that a firm cannot simultaneously maximise Cost, Speed, Flexibility and Quality performance, so a strategy must prioritise some dimensions and accept limits on others.
A value-chain strategy that prioritises customer experience and responsiveness in order fulfillment — speed, accuracy and flexibility — to justify premium pricing.
A value-chain strategy that prioritises efficient, low-cost order fulfillment that minimises waste, labour cost and shipping errors.
The Supply Chain Operations Reference model, which judges a whole supply-chain network on five performance attributes: Reliability, Responsiveness, Agility, Cost and Asset Management Efficiency.
The SCOR attribute measuring consistent, accurate and dependable supply-chain outcomes.
The SCOR attribute measuring how fast the supply chain delivers to customers.
The SCOR attribute measuring a supply chain's ability to adapt to changes in demand or supply.
A supply-chain strategy built on data-driven optimisation for e-commerce and tech-savvy firms, such as Amazon or JD.com.
A supply-chain strategy prioritising environmental and ethical impact, suited to eco-conscious brands such as Patagonia or IKEA.
Moving sourcing closer to the target market to reduce the lead-time and disruption risk that comes with global sourcing.
A temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service or result, ending when its objective is achieved, no longer needed, unachievable, or terminated by the sponsor.
The sequence of phases describing where a project is in its journey — Defining, Planning, Executing, Closing — across which uncertainty falls, knowledge grows, and the cost of change rises.
The PMBOK process group that defines and authorises a new project or phase.
The PMBOK process group that defines how the project's work will be done.
The PMBOK process group that performs the work defined by the plan.
The PMBOK process group that tracks performance and compares and adjusts, running continuously alongside Planning and Executing rather than after them.
The PMBOK process group that formally completes the project or phase.
The PMBOK knowledge area that pulls everything together: the charter, the single project management plan, integrated change control and trade-offs across other knowledge areas.
The PMBOK knowledge area covering what is in and out of the project, requirements, the WBS and preventing scope creep.
The PMBOK knowledge area covering activities, sequencing, durations, the critical path and dates.
The PMBOK knowledge area covering estimating, budgeting, and tracking spend against budget.
The PMBOK knowledge area covering acceptance criteria, standards, testing and defects.
The PMBOK knowledge area covering acquiring, developing and managing the project's internal people and equipment, called Human Resource Management in the older PMBOK edition.
The PMBOK knowledge area deciding what information goes to whom, in what format and how often.
The PMBOK knowledge area covering identifying, analysing, planning responses to, and monitoring uncertain future events.
The PMBOK knowledge area covering contracts, vendors and purchasing from external suppliers, as distinct from Resource Management, which covers people from inside the organisation.
The PMBOK knowledge area covering identifying, analysing and engaging the people affected by the project.

A short, high-level document that formally authorises a project and empowers the project manager to lead it, covering purpose, objective, high-level scope, deliverables, sponsor/PM, milestones/budget and major risks.
A person, group or organisation that can affect, be affected by, or perceive itself to be affected by the project.
A stakeholder need stated precisely enough to be built and tested, which then becomes a deliverable or feature.
A requirement stating what the deliverable must do, such as updating store inventory after every transaction.
The work required to create a project's agreed deliverables, answering what is delivered, what is included and what is excluded.
The features and functions that describe the result a project creates, as distinct from project scope, which describes the work required to create that result.
The document defining a project's objective, deliverables, requirements, in-scope work, out-of-scope work and acceptance criteria.
The specific, measurable conditions that determine whether a deliverable is acceptable, without which a deliverable is difficult to control.
The uncontrolled expansion of project scope without a corresponding adjustment to time, cost or resources.
Adding extra features or enhancements to a deliverable that are not necessary, done on the project team's own initiative.
A hierarchical decomposition of the project scope into smaller, manageable components down to the work package, which carries no sequencing information.
The lowest, most manageable level of a Work Breakdown Structure, small enough to be estimated, assigned to one owner, monitored and accepted.
The WBS principle that its components together represent 100% of the project scope, with no missing work and no work duplicated.

A responsibility matrix assigning Responsible (does the work), Accountable (owns the result), Consulted (gives input) and Informed (needs updates) to each work package, with exactly one Accountable owner per item.
A defined piece of project work that consumes time and usually resources, one level below a work package.
A significant project event or checkpoint with zero duration that marks a moment rather than consuming time.
A dependency in which the successor activity cannot start until the predecessor activity finishes; the default and most common dependency type.
A dependency in which the successor activity cannot start until the predecessor activity starts.
A dependency in which the successor activity cannot finish until the predecessor activity finishes.
A dependency in which the successor activity cannot finish until the predecessor activity starts.
A schedule overlap in which the successor activity starts before its predecessor has completely finished, compressing the schedule.
A deliberate wait inserted between two activities, stretching the schedule.
The amount of work an activity requires, such as 40 person-hours, which is not the same number or unit as its duration.
How long an activity takes on the calendar, such as 5 working days, distinct from the effort it requires.
A visual bar chart of activities against time, used to communicate schedule information such as start/finish, duration, lead/lag and milestones.
The earliest an activity can begin, computed on the forward pass as the maximum earliest finish of all its predecessors.
The earliest an activity can finish, computed on the forward pass as EF = ES + Duration.
The latest an activity can begin without delaying the project, computed on the backward pass as LS = LF - Duration.
The latest an activity can finish without delaying the project, computed on the backward pass as the minimum latest start of all its successors.
The amount of time an activity can be delayed without delaying project completion, equal to LS - ES (or LF - EF); a critical activity has a float of zero.
The longest sequence of dependent activities in a project network, made up of activities with zero float, where any delay pushes back the whole project.
The approved, time-phased budget used as the reference point for measuring actual project spend, plotted as a cumulative S-curve.
An uncertain future event or condition that may affect one or more project objectives, positively or negatively.
A problem that is currently and actually affecting the project, as distinct from a risk, which is only a future possibility.
A limiting factor that restricts project options or decisions and is always present, such as a fixed three-month deadline.
Something believed to be true without proof and used for planning, paired with the risk that the belief turns out to be wrong.
A task or event that relies on another to start, continue or finish, describing an ongoing relationship rather than a single point in time.
A flaw or bug in a deliverable, discovered after creation, that fails to meet quality standards.
A risk originating from money, such as budget overruns or resource misallocation.
A risk originating from technology, such as technology failure, underperformance, or an unsuitable technology choice.
A risk originating from how work is performed, such as poorly defined processes, inadequate staffing, or supplier delays.
A risk originating outside the organisation, such as regulation, market changes, or natural disasters.
A risk originating from the organisation's own structure or behaviour, such as scope creep, poor communication, or internal priority shifts.
A negative-risk response that eliminates the cause of a threat by removing the activities or people involved.
A positive-risk response that guarantees an opportunity occurs by adding the activities or people that cause it.
A negative-risk response that makes a third party accountable for a threat, such as through insurance or a fixed-price contract.
A positive-risk response that gives a third party a stake in an opportunity so they help capture it, such as through partnering.
A negative-risk response that reduces a threat's probability and/or impact, such as through training or a prototype.
A positive-risk response that increases an opportunity's probability and/or impact, such as through incentives.
A response, for either a threat or an opportunity, that takes no proactive action beyond acknowledging the risk.
The level of quality expected for a deliverable, such as sessions running on time to respect attendees' time.
How a deliverable's performance will be measured, such as the percentage of sessions starting within 5 minutes of schedule.
The specific, numeric level a metric must reach to be acceptable, such as at least 95% of sessions starting on time.
A preventive, process-focused check asking whether the right process is being followed.
A detective, output-focused check asking whether the deliverable meets requirements.
The sum of the cost of conformance (prevention and appraisal, spent to avoid failures) and the cost of nonconformance (internal and external failure costs, spent after failures happen).
